analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and lets people buy federal-employee health plans at their own cost.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by a single House member with no cosponsors, was referred to nine committees and never received a hearing or vote before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the Affordable Care Act and its companion 2010 law from the books, restoring the pre-2010 legal landscape. In its place, it would have the federal office that runs health insurance for government employees sign contracts with private insurers to offer similar plans to the general public. People enrolled in Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, or their own employer's plan could not buy in; everyone else could, but would pay the entire premium out of pocket, with a federal tax deduction to soften it. There would be no government contribution toward anyone's coverage.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, higher-income households would gain in two ways: the bill repeals the health-care provisions of the 2010 reconciliation law, which included the 3.8% tax on net investment income, and it makes premiums for the new plans fully tax-deductible, a benefit worth most to those who itemize and face high tax rates. Uninsured people ineligible for public programs would gain access to the federal-employee-style plans, though only by paying the full premium themselves. Insurers under contract with the federal employee program would gain a new, voluntary customer market.

how_it_helps.text: It would let anyone not eligible for Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, the federal employee program, or the uniformed services buy a federal-employee-style health plan through OPM-contracted carriers.
It would make premiums for these plans fully tax-deductible above the line, so itemizing taxpayers reduce their taxable income by what they pay.

By repealing the health-related provisions of the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010, it would eliminate the 3.8% tax on net investment income, which falls mainly on households with substantial capital gains and investment earnings.
It would allow premiums to vary by geographic region, so buyers in lower-cost areas could pay less.

analysis.who_pays: If it passed, the costs would fall on people who had come to rely on the Affordable Care Act: those receiving premium subsidies, the states' Medicaid expansion population, people with preexisting conditions who lost guaranteed access to coverage and community-rated prices, and seniors whose prescription-drug coverage gap had been closing. People buying the new plans would pay the full premium with no government contribution, and a tax deduction is worth least to those with low incomes.
analysis.who_pays_short: Subsidy recipients and people with preexisting conditions

drawbacks.text: Enrollees would receive no government contribution toward their premium, so coverage bought this way could be out of reach for low- and middle-income families even with the deduction.
Repeal would restore the law as it stood before 2010, when insurers could deny coverage or charge more based on health status, and when annual and lifetime coverage limits were legal.
A tax deduction for premiums delivers the largest benefit to households in higher tax brackets, doing least for the uninsured it is nominally aimed at.

Repealing the 2010 reconciliation law's health provisions would also unwind its Medicare changes, including the closed prescription-drug coverage gap and reductions in Medicare Advantage overpayments.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's practical offer to the uninsured — a way to buy a federal-employee-style plan — came with no subsidy, meaning many of the people losing Affordable Care Act coverage could not afford the replacement. The benefits skewed toward households with investment income and high tax bills. An honest supporter would acknowledge that the replacement did not attempt to preserve affordability guarantees for lower-income or sick people.

outcome.mechanism: One House member introduced the bill alone; it was sent to nine committees, bounced among health-related subcommittees for four months, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Darrell Issa introduced the bill on January 6, 2015, the first day of the new Congress, with no cosponsors.
The House referred it to nine committees, including Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means, for consideration of whichever provisions fell in each committee's jurisdiction.
Between February and April 2015 it was referred to health-related subcommittees in several committees, including the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health.
No committee reported the bill, no hearing or markup is recorded, and no vote was ever held in either chamber through the end of the 114th Congress on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the Affordable Care Act's premium subsidies, Medicaid expansion, and protections for people with preexisting conditions stayed in place, and the 3.8% tax on investment income remained in force. The sponsor gained a repeal statement on the record but no policy change.

for.name: Rep. Darrell Issa
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor.

against.name: House majority leadership
against.role: Controlled committee referrals and House floor scheduling
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to nine committees, where it stayed without a markup or floor vote for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican sponsored the bill, no member of either party cosponsored it, and no vote was ever taken, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: Repealing the health provisions of the 2010 reconciliation law would eliminate the 3.8% tax on net investment income, which applies mainly to capital gains and investment earnings of higher-income households. The cost side of the bill — loss of subsidies and protections — falls on lower-income people instead.

Insurers under contract with the federal employee health program would gain a new voluntary market of individual customers contracted through OPM. But repealing the Affordable Care Act would end the subsidized individual market and the mandate-driven expansion of covered customers, so the industry would gain one channel while losing another.

Repealing the 2010 reconciliation law's health provisions would restore the law as it stood before the payment reductions that law made to Medicare Advantage. That would return Medicare savings toward what private Medicare plans received, shifting costs back to taxpayers and beneficiaries.

Repeal of the Affordable Care Act would erase the annual fee it imposed on brand-name prescription drug manufacturers. The cost of that fee reduction is borne by the Medicare program and, indirectly, beneficiaries and taxpayers.
